key: For it is precept by precept, precept by precept, Line by line, line by line; Here a little, there a little.
s: With priest and prophet reeling from wine, the chapter asks whom one shall teach; Rashi, on 28:10, reads it as the people setting an idolatrous precept against each one the prophet brings, and holding theirs weightier, and Ibn Ezra, on 28:10, as speech fit for a small child, taught as writing is taught.

evidence.gloss: [Rashi, on 28:10, ‘precept by precept’:] The prophet commands them from the Holy One, blessed be He, and they have a precept of idolatry set against this precept; the prophet admonishes them again, and they always say, ‘We have a precept for the precept; ours is weightier than yours’ … [Ibn Ezra, on 28:10:] they are fit to be spoken to as a father speaks to his small son, who does not yet know … ‘Line by line’: the teaching of writing.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Isaiah 28:10, at [361,10]); one unit, no dash. Plain sense faithful: 28:7 priest and prophet reel through wine and strong drink, 28:9 asks whom one shall teach knowledge; the context clause does not repeat four words of the key. Rashi on 28:10 (lemma כי צו לצו צו לצו): the prophet brings a command from God and they set an idolatrous precept against it, always saying theirs is weightier; the sentence’s “against each one” renders Rashi’s “against this precept” with his “always”, without drift. Ibn Ezra on 28:10: they must be spoken to as a father speaks to a small son who does not yet know, and “line by line” is the teaching of writing; the sentence carries exactly that. The two genuinely differ (counter-precepts of the people versus the manner fit for children) and are named without resolving. Entry passes entry-check.
